pages.subtitle: The seventh California mission, known for its ruined stone church and its swallows, built on the homeland of the Acjachemen people.
pages.founding_source_note: Mission San Juan Capistrano, "History"; California Missions Foundation, "San Juan Capistrano." The display shows the year only, as the CSV and hub do.
pages.intro: Mission San Juan Capistrano was the seventh California mission. Saint Junípero Serra founded it in 1776 on the homeland of the Acjachemen people. It is famous for the ruins of a great stone church and for the swallows that fly back every spring. Its story also holds sadness. The Acjachemen lost their villages and their freedom, and an earthquake took many lives.
story_paragraphs: The Acjachemen (say it ah-HAWSH-eh-men) people have lived in the land now called Orange County for as long as 10,000 years. One of their main villages, Putuidem, stood close to where the mission is now. Families lived in houses covered with bark or reeds. Acorns and seeds made up more than half of their food.
In October 1775, Father Fermín Lasuén came to start a mission here. About a week later, news came of an attack on the mission at San Diego. The priests buried the mission bells and hurried away.

On November 1, 1776, Father Junípero Serra came back. The bells were dug up and hung from a tree, and the mission began again. It was the seventh California mission. It was named for Saint John of Capistrano, a Franciscan priest from Italy.
Soon a small adobe church was built. Today it is called the Serra Chapel. It is the last mission church still standing in which Father Serra celebrated Mass.

The Acjachemen were brought into the mission, and the Spanish gave them a new name, Juaneños. A tribal member named Jerry Nieblas says that one of his ancestors, Maria Bernarda Chigilia, lived at Putuidem. In 1776, she was taken from her land and not allowed to go back. At the mission, Native people worked making leather, soap, candles, and iron tools. Many grew sick and died.

In 1797, work began on a huge stone church with seven domes and a tall bell tower. It was finished in 1806. Then, in December 1812, an earthquake struck, and the church fell. Forty people were killed. The church was never rebuilt.

In 1845, the governor sold the mission to his brother-in-law. In 1865, President Abraham Lincoln gave it back to the Church. A priest named St. John O'Sullivan came in 1910 and spent many years repairing it.
The Acjachemen people are still here. Today, they teach their children their language and stories at a village park called Putuidem.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Acjachemen people. Before the mission, they lived in villages along the creeks and rivers of what is now Orange County. Each village led itself. People hunted, fished, and gathered acorns and seeds. When the mission came, the Acjachemen were baptized and given the name Juaneño, after the mission. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. The mission's own history says that about 65,000 Native people lived along the California coast in 1770, and that only about 17,000 were still living in 1830. Today, the tribe is called the Juaneño Band of Mission Indians, Acjachemen Nation. An elder named Joyce Perry teaches her granddaughter the Acjachemen words for the sun, the moon, the ocean, and the stars.
type_specific.mission_life: This was a busy mission. Workers tanned cattle hides into leather and melted fat to make soap and candles. They made shoes, hats, and blankets, pressed olives for oil, and grew grapes. The mission was the first in California to make iron from rock in hot furnaces. Its ranches covered most of what is now Orange County. The Acjachemen did this work because they had to. Their own way of life, in their own villages, had been taken from them.
type_specific.architecture: Two churches tell this mission's story. The Serra Chapel is a long, narrow adobe church from mission days. It was close to falling down by the 1890s and was repaired between 1910 and 1924. Its golden altar is very old, but it came from Spain in the 1920s. The Great Stone Church was made of yellow sandstone, with seven domes and a bell tower 120 feet tall. The broken walls you can see are the real ruins from 1812. They have never been rebuilt. Four bells saved from the tower hang in a low bell wall built in 1813. Many of the workshops in the courtyard are modern copies.

pages.subtitle: The eighth California mission, built on the Ohlone homeland called Thámien. Today it stands in the middle of a university.
pages.founding_source_note: Santa Clara University, "History of the Mission"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission Santa Clara.

pages.intro: Mission Santa Clara de Asís was the eighth California mission. It was founded in 1777 on the homeland of the Ohlone people, in a place they called Thámien. It was the first mission named for a woman saint. The mission had to be rebuilt many times. More than 7,500 Native people are buried there. Today, it is the church of Santa Clara University.
story_paragraphs: Before the Spanish came, about 10,000 Native people lived around the south end of San Francisco Bay, in as many as 40 separate tribes. One group of villages, home to about 300 to 500 people, stood in a place called Thámien. The people who come from them today call themselves Ohlone.

On January 12, 1777, a mission was founded beside the Guadalupe River. Father Junípero Serra had sent a priest named Tomás de la Peña, who set up a wooden cross. It was the eighth California mission. It was named for Saint Clare of Assisi, a friend of Saint Francis.
The river soon flooded, so the mission moved to higher ground. Later, earthquakes knocked down its churches. In all, five churches were built. The fifth was finished in 1825.

Mission life was very hard for the Ohlone. Santa Clara University says that they were forced to work long hours, plowing fields and digging ditches. The priests did not let them keep many of their customs. Some people went on speaking their language and holding their ceremonies in secret.

Many people died of sickness. As the years went by, Yokuts and Miwok people from far-off valleys and hills were brought to the mission too. By 1834, more than half the people there were Yokuts. More than 7,500 Native people are buried at the mission.
In 1836, the government took the mission away from the Church. In 1851, priests called Jesuits turned the old mission into a college. It became Santa Clara University.
In 1926, a fire destroyed the church of 1825. A new church was built by 1929 to look like the old one. It is made of concrete instead of adobe.
Today, the mission church stands at the center of the university. As the university says, "The Ohlone are here, still."

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands in Thámien, the homeland of one group of Ohlone people. Their villages shared one language with their neighbors around the bay. Native people built the mission buildings and did the farming and other work, and they were not free to refuse. Mission life also brought strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land, language, and freedom. In all, about 6,400 Native people were baptized here. About 4,450 of them were Ohlone, about 1,460 were Yokuts, and about 450 were Miwok. When the missions closed, few Native people were given any land. The Muwekma Ohlone Tribe of the San Francisco Bay Area is made up of families who come from the people of this mission and its neighbors. The tribe has given the Guadalupe River its Ohlone name again: Thámien Rúmmey.
type_specific.mission_life: At one time, more than 1,200 Native workers lived at the mission. They plowed, planted, dug ditches to water the fields, and cared for cattle and sheep. A priest named Magín Catalá lived here for 36 years. The mission also built a wide road to the nearby town of San José, with three rows of willow trees for shade. It was called The Alameda, and a street with that name is still there.
type_specific.architecture: The church you see today is not from mission days. It was built in the 1920s, after the fire, out of concrete and steel. It copies the shape of the 1825 adobe church, with one bell tower, but it is twice as wide. A few real pieces of the old mission are left. A long adobe wall from the 1820s still stands nearby. A large wooden cross on a stand in front of the church is said to hold the cross set up in 1777. One of the bells sent by the King of Spain in 1799 lived through the fire. Inside is a crucifix that students carried out of the burning church.

pages.subtitle: The ninth California mission and the last one Saint Junípero Serra founded, built by the sea on the homeland of the Chumash people.
pages.founding_source_note: Mission Basilica San Buenaventura, "History"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission San Buenaventura.
pages.intro: Mission San Buenaventura was the ninth California mission. Saint Junípero Serra founded it on Easter Sunday in 1782. It was the last mission he started before he died. The mission stands near the ocean on the homeland of the Chumash people, who were skilled boat builders. The Chumash built the mission and its long water channel. Sickness later took most of their people.
story_paragraphs: The Chumash people once numbered in the tens of thousands. Their homeland reached along the coast from Malibu to Paso Robles. They lived in round houses made of willow branches. They were the finest boat builders among the Native peoples of California. They made canoes out of wooden planks and sealed them with tar.

On Easter Sunday, March 31, 1782, Father Junípero Serra raised a cross near the beach and founded Mission San Buenaventura. It was the ninth California mission, and the last one he founded. He named it for Saint Bonaventure and left a priest named Pedro Cambón in charge.
Chumash workers built the first church quickly, but it burned down. A bigger church of stone and adobe was started in the 1790s. It took many years, and it was finished in 1809.

Between 1805 and 1815, the Chumash also built a water channel about seven miles long. It carried water from the river to the mission. With that water, the mission grew orchards and gardens. An English sea captain named George Vancouver called them the finest he had seen.
In 1812, earthquakes and a great wave from the sea struck the coast. The priests and the Chumash had to leave the mission for a while and live farther from shore.

The years of the missions were years of great loss for the Chumash. Sicknesses from Europe spread from person to person. The Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians says that about 22,000 Chumash lived in their homeland before the Spanish came. By 1831, the missions listed only 2,788.
In the 1830s, the government took the mission away from the Church. President Abraham Lincoln returned it in 1862. In 2020, Pope Francis named the church a basilica.
Chumash people still live in their homeland today. They are keeping their culture and their language alive.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Chumash people. Many elders say the name Chumash means "bead maker" or "seashell people." As many as 50 people could live in one of their large round houses. They fished, hunted, gathered plants, and stored food for winter. They held ceremonies at harvest time. The Chumash built this mission and its water channel. Mission life also brought forced work, strict rules, and the loss of land and freedom, and sickness killed most of the people. After the missions closed, most Chumash who stayed nearby worked on farms and ranches. Today, the Chumash are still here. One band of Chumash families in this area is called the Barbareño/Ventureño Band of Mission Indians.
type_specific.mission_life: Water made this mission rich. The channel filled a stone tank, and from there water ran to the orchards, vineyards, and fields of grain. The mission grew pears and even warm-weather fruits like bananas. Chumash workers did the building, farming, and herding. An early report says that many Chumash here chose to stay in their own homes near the mission instead of moving inside it.
type_specific.architecture: The church is made of stone and adobe, with walls more than six feet thick. It is the same church that was finished in 1809. After the earthquake of 1812 knocked down the bell tower, the tower was rebuilt with a thick stone support. In 1893, a priest changed the inside to make it look modern. He covered the old painted designs, the tile floor, and the wooden ceiling. In the 1950s, workers uncovered the floor and ceiling and made the windows their old size again. The church is the only building left from the mission. The mission also has two rare bells made of wood.

pages.subtitle: The tenth California mission, called the "Queen of the Missions," built on the homeland of the Chumash people.
pages.founding_source_note: California Missions Foundation, "Santa Bárbara"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission Santa Barbara.
pages.intro: Mission Santa Bárbara was the tenth California mission. Father Fermín Lasuén founded it in 1786 on the homeland of the Chumash people. It is the only California mission with two matching bell towers, and people call it the "Queen of the Missions." The Chumash built it. In 1824, Chumash people at this mission and two others rose up against the soldiers.
story_paragraphs: The Chumash have lived along the Santa Barbara coast for thousands of years. They built round houses shaped like half an orange and covered them with reeds. They paddled plank canoes called tomols out to the islands. Acorns were their most important plant food, and they ate fish and shellfish from the sea. For money, they used strings of small beads cut from shells.

Father Junípero Serra wanted a mission here, but he died before it could begin. On December 4, 1786, the feast day of Saint Barbara, Father Fermín Lasuén founded Mission Santa Bárbara. It was the tenth California mission.

The Chumash built the mission's buildings. They also built dams, stone channels, and tanks that brought water down from a creek. Many Chumash families lived in about 250 small adobe houses beside the mission.

In 1812, an earthquake badly damaged the church. A new church of stone was built from 1815 to 1820. Its front was copied from a very old book about Roman buildings in the mission library. A second bell tower was added in 1831.
Life at the mission was hard. Sickness spread, food and supplies ran short, and the Chumash had to feed and support the soldiers as well as themselves.

In February 1824, a soldier at nearby Mission Santa Inés whipped a Chumash man. That was the last straw. Chumash people at three missions, Santa Inés, La Purísima, and Santa Bárbara, took up arms. The struggle lasted for months. At least 43 Native people and 8 settlers died.
In 1835, the government took the mission lands away. The Franciscan priests stayed, and they have never left. About 4,000 Chumash people are buried at the mission.
An earthquake damaged the church again in 1925, and it was repaired by 1927. Chumash people still live in the Santa Barbara area today and gather each year to remember their ancestors of 1824.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Chumash people. Before the missions, two out of three Chumash lived near the coast, in towns led by chiefs. People on the islands made shell bead money and traded it to the mainland. The Chumash wove baskets so tight they could hold water. When the mission came, many Chumash were baptized and moved beside it. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. In 1824, the Chumash resisted. A Chumash woman named Marianne Parra says she grew up knowing that story her whole life. Each year, she and a Chumash elder, Ernestine Ygnacio-DeSoto, hold a ceremony to remember the ancestors and say their names.
type_specific.mission_life: Water ran through the middle of mission life. It flowed from the dams to a fountain in front of the church. From the fountain it filled a long stone pool where the women washed clothes. Chumash workers farmed, herded animals, and built with adobe and stone. In 1818, about 150 mission workers were trained to help guard the coast when a pirate ship was near. For many years, the mission was also a school for young men studying to be Franciscan priests.
type_specific.architecture: The stone church has a front that looks like an ancient Roman temple, with tall columns. Above it rise two matching bell towers, each 87 feet tall. No other California mission has two towers like these. The church is the one finished in 1820, but it has been repaired many times. The earthquake of 1925 broke the towers and walls, and they were fixed by 1927. The towers were made stronger with steel and concrete in 1948. The stone fountain and washing pool in front are from mission days.

pages.subtitle: The eleventh California mission, destroyed by an earthquake and rebuilt twice, on the homeland of the Chumash people.
pages.founding_source_note: California State Parks, "Community Through Survival: La Purísima Mission State Historic Park"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission La Purísima Concepción.
pages.intro: Mission La Purísima Concepción was the eleventh California mission. Father Fermín Lasuén founded it in 1787 on the homeland of the Chumash people. An earthquake destroyed it in 1812, and it was built again in a new place. In 1824, the Chumash took over the mission for about a month. Today, it is a state park where the whole mission has been rebuilt.
story_paragraphs: The Chumash people have lived on this part of the California coast for thousands of years. They fished, hunted, gathered acorns, and built canoes out of wooden planks.

On December 8, 1787, Father Fermín Lasuén founded Mission La Purísima Concepción. Its name honors Mary, the mother of Jesus. It was the eleventh California mission. The first mission stood where the town of Lompoc is today, and it grew there for about 25 years.

In 1812, a great earthquake struck. Then came more shaking and a flood. Every building was ruined. The priest in charge, Father Mariano Payeras, asked to move the mission to a valley about four miles away. Building began there in 1813.
The new mission looked different. The buildings stood in one long line instead of around a square. That may have been so people could get out fast in an earthquake.

Life was hard for the Chumash at the mission. A state park guide says that sickness was everywhere and many people died. The work grew heavier, too, because the soldiers were not being paid and the mission had to supply them.

In February 1824, a soldier at nearby Mission Santa Inés whipped a Chumash man. The Chumash rose up. At La Purísima, they sent the soldiers and their families away and ran the mission themselves for about a month. Then more soldiers came from Monterey, pulling cannons. After a battle at the mission, the soldiers took it back.
In 1834, the government took the mission away from the Church. The buildings were left empty and slowly fell apart, until only pieces of the walls were left.

In 1934, about 200 young men from a government work program called the Civilian Conservation Corps began to rebuild the mission. They made adobe bricks by hand, the old way. The work took seven years. Today, the mission is a state historic park, and Chumash people still live in their homeland.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Chumash people. The Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians says that Chumash society had chiefs, healers, and skilled craftspeople, and that women could be chiefs and priests. The Chumash painted colorful pictures on the walls of caves. When the mission came, many Chumash were baptized. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. In 1824, the Chumash resisted and held this mission for about a month. In that uprising, at least 43 Native people and 8 settlers died at the three missions that took part. Today, the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians lives nearby. They are working to keep their culture and their language, called Samala, strong for the children to come.
type_specific.mission_life: La Purísima was a working ranch as well as a church. It had more than 20,000 cattle, sheep, and other animals. Workers stored hides and animal fat to trade, boiled soap in big tubs, and wove wool into blankets. The blankets were what the mission was best known for. There were workshops for blacksmiths, carpenters, potters, and leather workers. Chumash people did nearly all of this work.
type_specific.architecture: Almost everything at La Purísima today was rebuilt in the 1930s. A state park guide puts it plainly: "Everything you see around you has been reconstructed." Only broken pieces of the old adobe walls were left, and the builders kept those pieces inside the new walls. The bell wall is a copy of the one at Mission Santa Inés, because no one had a picture of the first one. A few things are from mission days. The three bronze bells were made in Lima, Peru, in 1817 and 1818. Part of a tile floor is old, too. The long, straight line of buildings follows the plan of 1813.

quiz.prompt: What number was this mission in the order the missions were founded?
quiz.explanation: Mission La Purísima Concepción, founded on December 8, 1787, was the eleventh of the 21 California missions.

quiz.prompt: Which Native people's homeland is the mission built on?
quiz.explanation: The mission was built on the homeland of the Chumash people. The Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians lives nearby today.

quiz.prompt: What destroyed the first mission in 1812?
quiz.explanation: A great earthquake, more shaking, and a flood ruined every building. The mission was rebuilt about four miles away.

quiz.prompt: How are this mission's buildings arranged?
quiz.explanation: Most missions were built around a square courtyard. At La Purísima, the buildings stand in a line.

quiz.prompt: Who rebuilt the ruined mission in the 1930s?
